title: Articulation: two kinds of touch
summary: Play staccato notes short and detached, legato notes smooth and joined, like two different voices.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil

figure.alt: A bar of eight beats: the first four short and separated, each with a rest after it, the way a staccato note is played; the last four are one note held smoothly across three beats, the way a legato line is played.

steps.title: Articulation: two kinds of touch
steps.body:
Staccato means short and separated, each note lifted quickly like a spoken word on its own. Legato means smooth and joined, each note flowing into the next with no gap, like a sung line. The same notes played the two ways tell completely different stories.

1. Find a bar marked staccato and play it short, lifting each finger quickly after the key goes down.
2. Find a bar marked legato and play it connected, holding each note until the very next one begins.
3. Play one bar both ways, staccato then legato, and listen closely to the difference.
4. Play the whole piece, exaggerating the difference at first, then settling it back to a natural amount.

Articulation is the difference between a piece that sounds like it is being read aloud and one that sounds like it is speaking.

figure.alt: The same bar, short and separated notes then one smooth held note, played back to back so the two touches, staccato then legato, can be heard right after each other.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: find every staccato and legato marking, play three bars of each slowly
Sitting 2: play one bar both ways in a row, staccato then legato
Sitting 3: the hard bars with their articulation, slowly, then at tempo
Sitting 4: the whole piece with its articulation, then once as if recording
An old piece played once, adding articulation it never had marked
